dplyr
dplyr uses different verbs to work with tibbles.

filter() picks rows
select() picks columns
mutate() adds a new computed column:


new <- mutate(counties, income2)


arrange() changes the order of rows
group_by() + summarize() many rows become few

For example:



County
State
Income




Orange

70,000


Nassau
NY
80,000

CA
90,000


Sacramento
CA
100,000



Becomes:



State
Income




NY
70,000


CA
80,000




Pipe operator |>
We can think of |> as saying “and then…”
To use the pipe operator, we use ⌘ + Shift + M.

new_data <- counties |> 
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |> 
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |> 
  select(NAME, moe_pct)

title: Week 2: Getting started with R
Week 2: Getting started with R
text:
The Census
Decennial Census: Mandated by the Constitution, conducted every 10 years with 10 questions.
American Community Survey (ACS): Created in 2005, more interesting questions! Approximately 3% of households are surveyed about income, rent, home value, commute time, ethnicity, etc. From that sample, we come up with an estimate for the population.

1-year ACS: Almost never used, only for places > 65,000 people. Most current, comes out every year.
5-year ACS: Block Group, Census Tract. If you get ACS data for the year 2016, it is a 5 year average. These are estimates +- a margin of error. It is NOT just an estimate for 2016, but for the interval of 2011-2016.


Census Code

B19013_001E or B19013_001M

B: Base table
19013: Table #
001: Line Number
E: Estimate
M: Margin of Error

The command load_variables() shows us the name of our variables. All of this exists in a library called tidycensus().



Census Geography

State -> County -> Tract (“Neighborhood”) -> Block Groups (HORRIBLE margins of error!) -> Block (Decennial Census only)
About 5,000-8,000 people
Boundaries of census tracts change over time! To mitigate this, there are longitudinal tract databases



GEOID
A GEOID is a unique identifier for a census tract.

First two numbers is the state
Next three numbers is the county
Last six digits are the census tract

A GEOID is stored as string. This is important, as there are states such as Alabama with a 01 state identifier.


Using tidycensus()

data <- get_acs(geography: 'county',
                variables = c('B1013_001',
                              'B01003_001'),
                state = 'PA',
                year = 2023,
                survey = 'acs5',
                output = 'wide') #To get our data in wide format 

When we run this command, we receive it in tidy format, with multiple rows for each county (each row shows a different variable value –> “variable” itself is a column). We want to turn it into wide format, with different variables in each column.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.






TipDelete this box



Rewrite the paragraph below in your own words once you’ve picked your state and variable. Two or three sentences saying what you’re looking at and why.


In this analysis, I look at [YOUR VARIABLE] across counties in [YOUR STATE], and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = ___ / ___ * 100)







NoteDelete this box



Fill in the two blanks. You want: how big is the margin of error, relative to the estimate, as a percentage?


Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)







TipDelete this box



Write a sentence or two naming the least reliable county and its moe_pct.


[Which county has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate? How large is it?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)







NoteDelete this box



Those cutoffs (5% and 10%) are a bit of a judgment call, not a law of nature. If almost every county lands in one category, adjust them so the split is informative for your variable — then say in your writing that you changed them and why. (I have a feeling for county-level, you may end up in high confidence everywhere - is smaller geographies where it really shows up. So feel free to change those numbers around a bit)


[How many counties fall into each category?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)







NoteDelete this box



Notice the column names: myvarE, myvarM, popE, popM. The E and M suffixes are estimate and margin of error.



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(___) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(___)
  )







NoteDelete this box



Two blanks. What are you grouping by? What are you averaging?








TipDelete this box



This table is the heart of the assignment. Describe what it shows in two or three sentences.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.
